title: 15-minute opening-range breakout — 19 gate/exit variants
data: FTMO index CFD 1m; OOS extended to 2026-07-28 for the final re-score
headline: 0 robust survivors from 19 variants. Out-of-sample expectancy of the base rule is about −$0.13/trade. The one walk-forward pass (prior-day OR bias) flipped to −$263.79 once 2.3 more forward months arrived, with 5 straight losing months.
why: The breakout direction carries almost no information on index CFDs, and what little there is is smaller than the spread. Gates and exits reshape the distribution but not the mean.
lesson: Changing the filter or the exit of a dead entry produces many correlated draws of one bet, not many independent tests. Count mechanisms, not variants.
summary: We tested the classic 15-minute opening-range breakout on the Nasdaq, S&P and Dow CFDs with 19 different filters and exits. None survived out of sample. The single version that passed walk-forward went on to lose over the next few months of fresh data.

title: 5-minute ORB with fair-value-gap confirmation (Reddit)
headline: Pooled net −0.66bp/trade (t=−2.11, n=3,503). Win rate 41% vs the poster's ~56%. The FVG filter made the bare breakout worse.
why: The FVG confirmation removes good breakouts as often as bad ones; the net result is negative after costs.
summary: A popular Reddit setup — trade the 5-minute opening-range break only when it leaves a fair-value gap — lost money across seven markets. The FVG filter made results worse than the plain breakout.

title: Reddit EMA-stack scalp — 4m EMA(5/9/30) + VWAP alignment
headline: Screen pooled −1.08bp/trade (t=−1.96), cost-negative on 6/7 markets. Walk-forward OOS Sharpe US100 −0.68, US500 −0.03.
why: A random-direction control did as well as the signal — the result is stop/target geometry, not direction.
summary: A Reddit EMA-stack / VWAP scalp lost money on 6 of 7 markets, and a coin-flip entry with the same stops did just as well.

title: First half-hour predicts the last half-hour (Gao et al. 2018)
headline: Gross edge absent — US100 +0.10pt against 1.47pt cost; US500/US30 negative before costs. Pooled net −1.23bp/trade (t=−1.99).
why: The published effect does not show up in recent index CFD data at all.
summary: The academic "intraday momentum" effect — the first 30 minutes predicting the last 30 — was not present in recent Nasdaq, S&P or Dow data, even before trading costs.

why: A wide stop does keep costs to ~1% of risk, but the signal itself is too weak to be distinguished from noise.
summary: An ATR volatility-breakout rule had the right directional tilt, but it was too weak to separate from noise and turned negative once spreads were doubled.

why: The edge is fragile and instrument-specific (BTCUSD and US30 deeply negative), and does not survive correction for the number of exits tried.
summary: A breakout that only starts trailing after +2R looked good out of sample on two indices, but not once we corrected for how many exits were tried — and it lost badly on Bitcoin and the Dow.

title: 30-minute ORB with EMA(9) trailing hold ("~95% win rate" method)
source: A trader's published method, sent to me (two filters withheld)
headline: Net-negative on all three indices; random direction did as well as the rule. Walk-forward OOS US100 +0.71, US500 −0.83.
why: The high advertised win rate is what a trailing stop does to any entry, not evidence of an edge.
lesson: A tight trailing stop converts small wins into a high win rate and leaves the average unchanged or worse.
summary: A 30-minute breakout sold on a ~95% win rate lost money on all three US indices. The high win rate came from the trailing stop, not the entry.

title: Reddit "simplest ORB" — NY 15m OR, close-confirm, wide stop
headline: First ORB to clear the cost screen (TRUE +13.69pt ≫ RANDOM +4.11 ≫ FADE −13.69 on US100), but over 8.4 years of QQQ the direction premium washes to +0.0bp and inverts in 2018 and 2020.
why: The short sample was one bull regime; the "edge" was trend beta.
lesson: A direction test that passes in one regime cannot see regime beta — always test through bear markets.
summary: A wide-stop 15-minute ORB looked genuinely directional on two years of bull-market data. Across eight years including 2018 and 2020 the edge disappeared and reversed in the sharp sell-offs.

why: The premium is about one spread wide; the $40K/yr claim needs a free venue plus discretionary bias.
summary: A Reddit prop-trading ORB + FVG setup claiming ~$40K a year made about +0.05R per trade before costs — not significant — and lost money after the spread. A 17-cell sweep of its levels found nothing either.

lesson: Re-fit on the early data and score the late data before trusting any post-hoc stack.

title: Noise-Area intraday momentum (Zarattini, Aziz & Barbon)
headline: CFD screen 5/6 — in-sample +2.13bp/session (t=+1.90), post-publication +2.10bp (t=+0.88, underpowered). On NQ futures at today's cost 2010–26: t=+3.59, Sharpe 0.85, but the registered 2010–22 holdout failed (net t=0.72) because historical micro-futures costs were 3–6× higher.
why: The effect is real (right direction, stronger in bear markets) but it is small, and the pre-registered holdout failed. A stop-and-daily-cap variant (V2) is a paper-trade candidate only.
lesson: A post-publication sample can be too short to confirm an effect that has not shrunk — compute the years needed before judging.
summary: The Noise-Area momentum paper is the strongest intraday result we have found. The direction is real and holds up in bear markets, but the edge is small. It failed our pre-registered holdout, so for now it is a paper-trading candidate on Nasdaq futures, not a validated strategy.

title: Reddit 1-min / 2-min ORB scalp at fixed 3:1
data: FTMO tick data (519 sessions US500) + 1m bars ~27 months
headline: Win rate 26.1% [22.6–29.9%], mean +0.008R, t=+0.10. The claimed 34–36% win rate is outside the confidence interval.
why: A 3:1 bracket wins ~25% of the time on a coin flip; the observed rate is the null. Break direction is real (TRUE−FADE +0.308R, t=+2.50) but smaller than the spread.
lesson: Before believing any win rate on a fixed R:R bracket, compare it with 1/(1+RR).
summary: A Reddit 1-minute ORB scalp at 3:1 claimed a 34–36% win rate. On real tick data it won 26% — exactly what a coin flip gives a 3:1 bracket. The breakout direction is real, but it is worth less than the spread.

title: A vendor's "5min ORB playbook on ES" (claimed 72% win rate, +108% in 6 months)
source: An ORB analytics vendor's marketing PDF
timeframe: 5m opening range, target 50% / stop 100% of the range
headline: US500 (the ES proxy): 544 trades, net −1.42pt/trade, t=−2.97, profit factor 0.72 — negative before costs. US100: net −0.34pt/trade, t=−0.13.
why: Target and stop are fractions of each day's range, so average winners were only ~0.34× average losers; the 72% vs 66.7% break-even argument hides that skew. The claim came from one 6-month window with day-of-week filters fitted on it.
summary: A vendor's 5-minute ORB for ES claimed a 72% win rate and +108% in six months. On two years of S&P data the same rule lost money before costs: winners were about a third the size of losers, which the win-rate pitch hides.

title: Initial-balance breakout by rejection + "ending zone" (IB75 pullback)
headline: The directional bias is real — the first-formed side broke first in 79–86% of sessions vs a 25–29% baseline (p<0.0001). The mechanical 1:1R pullback trade won 45–54%, a coin flip.
why: Waiting for the retrace to the 75% level throws away the information in the signal.
lesson: A real session-level signal can still be untradeable if the entry rule resets the odds.
summary: A vendor's "ending zone" observation is real — we reproduced it at 80–86% on four markets. But the trade taken off it (a pullback to the 75% level with a 1:1 target) wins about half the time, which is breakeven before costs.

title: ATR Fibonacci level ladder — gate, trigger box and chop-zone setups
source: A trading-education site built on a popular public ATR-levels indicator
headline: 16/16 tests reject. The site's statistics reproduce, but they are one-sided touch rates. "Gate completes 62.5%" becomes 35.2% as a trade vs a 38.2% coin flip (−0.058R, t=−1.66).
why: A touch probability with no opposing stop is not a win rate; several headlines also pool days that open already past the level.
lesson: Pooling gap-over days manufactured t=+19 on one test; a filter defined by what happens after entry cannot be traded.
summary: This site's numbers are honest — we reproduced them. The problem is what they measure: how often price touches a level, with no stop on the other side. Scored as real trades, 16 of 16 setups were no better than a coin flip.

summary: SMT divergence between the Nasdaq and S&P carried no directional information. The full ICT stack produced only 13 trades in 27 months across three indices, all losing.

summary: Sweeping external liquidity and targeting the nearest fair-value gap made nothing before costs on ~30,000 trades, and random entries did as well.

title: NQ sweep → market-structure shift → FVG framework
source: A free NQ framework from a trading-education site
headline: Pooled gross +0.033R (t=+0.65) even at zero cost. On resolved trades it hit target 18.7% vs a 22.3% random-walk baseline (z=−3.25); US100 −0.24R, t=−2.53.
why: It reaches its own structural target less often than a coin flip; the break-even look comes from trades timing out at the close.
lesson: A time-stopped bracket must be scored on resolved trades only — the naive test read z=+8.42, a false pass.
summary: A free sweep → market-structure shift → FVG framework reached its target less often than a coin flip would. It was flat even before costs, so trading it on cheaper futures would not help.

title: 5-minute OR failed-breakout fade — fixed-% risk, options, futures venue
source: A setup I was sent, re-tested
headline: Direction is real (wins 45.5% vs a 42.6% random-walk null, z=+3.52), but gross +0.0824R against 0.0808R of cost — a break-even multiplier of 1.02×. Net +0.0016R, +4.8R total vs a 182R drawdown.
why: The edge is one spread wide and sits in tiny-wick setups that cannot be filled at the modelled price; with a 15%-of-range stop floor it is −0.0088R before any cost.
lesson: A product wrapper multiplies edge and cost together; futures round trips are commission-dominated, so the saving is NQ-only and micros cost more per point than their parent.
summary: Fading failed 5-minute opening-range breaks has a real directional edge — but it is almost exactly one spread wide. Options make it worse, and even Nasdaq futures are not cheap enough to rescue it.

title: Systematic discovery — intraday FX and crypto bar patterns (Runs 003–005)
headline: 7 of 9 patterns reproduced out of sample (EURUSD t=12 in-sample; holdout t=3.2–5.6), but every one was 4–13× short of the spread. The edge is a one-time shift, flat from 1 to 96 bars.
why: Short-horizon reversal is real and is bid-ask bounce — by definition uncapturable. Passive limit entry was worse (adverse selection).
lesson: Report "does it repeat" and "does it pay" separately — they are different questions.
summary: Short-term reversal in FX and crypto is one of the most reliable patterns we have measured — it repeated out of sample in 7 of 9 cases. It is also 4–13 times smaller than the spread, because it is mostly the bid-ask bounce itself.

title: Bitcoin and gold intraday overextension reversion
headline: Bitcoin hourly autocorrelation ≈0 (t≈0.3–0.6), edge entirely in 2026; gold ~zero gross edge against a $40 round trip.
why: The intraday friction wall extends to crypto and gold.
summary: Fading big intraday moves in Bitcoin and gold did not work: there was no measurable reversion in Bitcoin and nothing before costs in gold.

why: A long-documented short-term reversal premium in US equity indices that survives costs because the hold is multi-day.
summary: Buying the Nasdaq, S&P and Dow after a sharp two-day drop (RSI(2) oversold) and holding a few days passed our full out-of-sample test, including real overnight financing costs.

title: Implied-vol-gated dip-buy
source: A trading-education blog (same author as S006)
data: 15y IBKR daily; CBOE VXN/VIX/VXD as the IV proxy
headline: Real alpha (TRUE +$30.99/trade t=+1.88 > RANDOM +$8.84 > FADE −$30.33) but return correlation +0.83 to +0.94 with daily_reversal.
why: A higher-frequency restatement of the same edge, and worse in crashes (US30 −629 pts below the 200-day average vs +128 for daily_reversal).
summary: Gating dip-buys on implied volatility produced a real edge, but it was the same edge as plain RSI(2) dip-buying and did worse in crashes — the opposite of the author's claim.

title: "Buy the Dip" — close > SMA200 + RSI(5) < 20, hold 5 days, on indices
source: A trading-education blog (same author as S006)
headline: Edge real (+74.2bp/trade, t=+5.00; ATR-strength claim replicates) but correlated with daily_reversal (0.41–0.70) and lower frequency.
why: The SMA200 filter avoids bear markets by not trading them, rather than improving bear-market results.
summary: The classic "buy the dip above the 200-day" rule works on index CFDs (+74bp per trade), but it is a slower, correlated version of RSI(2) dip-buying rather than a new edge.

title: "Buy the Dip" on 260 US single stocks (IBKR, the article's native design)
source: A trading-education blog (same author as S006)
headline: Edge real (DSR 0.972, TRUE +32.2bp > RANDOM +16.9 > FADE −44.3) but portfolio Sharpe 0.56 vs SPY 0.73; CAPM alpha +2.65%/yr at t=0.47.
why: It does not beat buy-and-hold, and Sharpe is leverage-invariant so sizing up cannot fix it. The edge also lives in survivors.
lesson: The first result where cost was not the binding constraint — the strategy failed on merit.
summary: Buying oversold US stocks works — but over 2010–2026 it earned less than just holding SPY, with a similar amount of risk. Its genuine strength is defence: in 2022 it lost 9.7% against SPY's 19.5%.

title: "Buy ES Monday 06:00 ET, sell 16:00 ET" claim
data: 16y SPY/QQQ daily; FTMO US500 1m incl. off-hours bars
headline: The 06:00 leg measured +$2,040/Monday (t=+2.74) — about 20 index points of which was a CFD quoting step at 09:30 ET (+27.75bp in one minute). The RTH part is the known Monday effect; after correcting for best-of-5 weekdays, p=0.61 (SPY) / 0.090 (QQQ).
why: The novel part was a data artefact; the rest was already known and borderline.
lesson: Profile a suspected level offset minute by minute before trusting a two-point decomposition; when scanning many buckets, gate on effect size — max |t| over 1,380 buckets reaches 4 by chance 14% of the time.
summary: A "buy ES at 6am Monday" claim looked significant, but most of the pre-market profit was a quoting artefact in the CFD data at the 9:30 open. The regular-hours part is the familiar Monday effect, and it is borderline once you account for picking the best day of the week.

title: Pre-FOMC overnight drift (Lucca & Moench)
timeframe: 1m, close before FOMC day → next open
headline: Drift alive in the overnight gap into FOMC day (US100 +27.5bp t=4.04, US500 +14.0bp t=3.74). Gate: TEST drawdown 0.90%, direction TRUE +6.65bp ≫ RANDOM −3.28; DSR 0.886 — one event carries 62% of TEST profit.
why: A documented pre-announcement premium; only ~8 trades a year, so the sample is thin.
summary: US indices have tended to gap up overnight into Federal Reserve announcement days. The effect is strong in the data but happens only about eight times a year, so one event dominates the recent sample.

title: Month-of-year long (April / July / November)
headline: Cleared the alpha gate (net Sharpe +0.379, 3/3, DSR 0.972) but ~2 trades/yr and large intra-month drawdown; standalone P(pass) ~27%.
why: Low frequency, correlated with the long-equity book, and it lowered the combined book's pass probability.
summary: Holding US indices only in April, July and November passed our statistical test, but with two trades a year and big swings inside the month it was not useful for a prop challenge.

title: Scheduled macro-announcement premium (FOMC + CPI + NFP days)
source: Savor & Wilson 2013; Lucca & Moench 2015; Ai & Bansal 2018
headline: Event days +5.80bp vs unconditional +5.69bp (Welch t=+0.03); negative since 2021; 0/5 criteria.
why: A post-publication death of the 1958–2009 result; only the FOMC overnight leg (S073) survives.
summary: The academic "announcement-day premium" — stocks earning far more on CPI, jobs and Fed days — was absent in 2015–2026 data. Announcement days returned the same as any other day.

title: Option-expiration week premium (third-Friday week)
data: 15y IBKR daily (2,649 pooled OE sessions); FTMO CFD confirm
headline: OE days +0.97bp vs non-OE +3.68bp (t=−1.38); a random week beats the OE week; 0/6 criteria; the "weak fourth week" is the best week.
why: Absent to inverted at index level, and dead since 2021.
summary: The idea that stocks do well in options-expiration week did not hold for US indices over 15 years — a randomly chosen week did better.

title: Pre-holiday effect (day before US market holidays)
headline: Pooled net +7.73bp (t=+2.31), 2.7× an ordinary day, alive since 2021 — but pre-holiday vs other days Welch t=+1.57 < 1.64.
why: The premium is present and holiday-specific; ~10 events a year is not enough power. Revisit with ≥3 more years.
summary: The day before a US market holiday has been about 2.7× stronger than a normal day since 2011. It falls just short of significance — with only ten holidays a year, it needs more data.

title: Gotobi Tokyo-fix USDJPY drift
headline: The shape exists (gross +0.99bp t=+2.31, post-fix reversal −1.36bp) but ~0.5bp gross vs a ~1.05bp round trip; decayed post-publication.
why: Real but sub-cost — the friction wall at sub-basis-point scale.
summary: The Japanese "gotobi" dollar-yen drift before the Tokyo fix is still visible, but it is about half the size of the spread and has faded since it was published.

title: Month-end WM/R London 4pm fix rebalancing flow
headline: Fingerprint present (signed pre-fix +3.06bp vs +0.66 ordinary; reversal −2.13bp t=−2.55) but pooled net +1.96bp t=+1.25; negative at 3× cost.
why: Real-looking but too small and noisy against FX costs.
summary: Month-end FX rebalancing around the London 4pm fix leaves a visible footprint, but it is too small to trade profitably after costs.

title: Bitcoin US-session / ETF-hours drift
headline: Inverted — post-ETF US hours −9.81bp/session on BTC (rest of day +11.52bp), ETH −30.86bp (t=−2.97).
why: The ETF era reversed the pattern the headlines describe, and it is getting worse.
summary: The popular claim that Bitcoin's gains happen during US trading hours since the ETFs launched is backwards in the data: those hours have been negative.

title: Bitcoin closed-exchange window — long 21:00→23:00 UTC
data: Binance 2017–2019 (unpeeked), FTMO BTCUSD 2023–2026; 40 post-freeze forward trades
verdict_label: ❌ Passed the gate, failed the forward test
headline: Strongest gate pass in the project (DSR 0.980, TEST +7.16bp/day t=+3.27, unpeeked 2017–19 +11.91bp). Forward test: 40 trades at −$7.21 vs a +$61.62 baseline — its own abort condition.
why: The edge did not survive real out-of-sample time; the data replayed to the cent, so it was not an artefact.
lesson: A high DSR on a walk-forward gate is not sufficient — only a forward test is.
summary: Our strongest backtest ever — Bitcoin's 21:00–23:00 UTC window — passed every statistical test, then lost money in live forward testing. It is the clearest lesson we have that a great backtest is not proof.

title: Overnight return anomaly — hold close→open
headline: Gross-positive on US100 and clears the spread, but pooled t=1.43 even at zero swap, and decaying.
why: Not significant, and sensitive to overnight financing.
summary: Holding US indices only overnight made a little on the Nasdaq, but not enough to be significant, and overnight financing costs erase it.

title: Time-of-day window sweep — 134 clock-anchored intraday rules
source: Heston, Korajczyk & Sadka 2010; Bogousslavsky 2016; Baltussen et al. 2021

headline: Best of 134 (10:00→16:00 prior-day fade) +5.24bp t=2.39 vs a required t≥3.0; its CFD confirm t=0.21.
why: No every-day intraday window survives multiple-testing correction; this closed the last every-day intraday family on FTMO CFDs.
summary: We swept 134 "buy at time X, sell at time Y" intraday windows. None beat what chance produces when you test that many, and the best one did not hold up on the tradeable CFD.

title: Overnight gap fade (gap_fade)
headline: First strategy ever to pass walk-forward; shelved the same day — both OOS legs one trade from negative, and decaying.
why: The pass rested on a single trade on each leg.
lesson: This is why the drop-the-best-trade check exists.
summary: Fading big overnight gaps was the first idea to pass our walk-forward test — and was shelved the same day, because removing one trade on each index turned it negative.

title: Quality-ETF pullback + 4H 200-EMA reclaim (LEAP swing blueprint, ETF leg)
source: A research blueprint I was sent
data: IBKR 4H 2010-08→2026-08 (21 ETFs); options layer blocked — no IBKR option history
headline: Technical-exit version flat vs its duration-matched null (t=+0.13). A fixed 3-month hold: n=50, +7.39%/trade, t=+2.35 vs its own null, 82% win, DSR 1.000 over the 4 hold lengths.

lesson: Compare each holding period with a null of the same length; a single 252-day baseline hid this and mis-judged every short hold.
summary: Buying quality ETFs after a pullback and a 200-EMA reclaim, then simply holding three months, is our most interesting swing lead: +7.4% per trade and clearly better than random. It came out of an exploratory search, so it still needs a clean pre-registered test.

why: The sweep-plus-gap entry carries no timing information: trades that hit stop or target won 30.3% vs a 33.3% coin-flip rate at 2R, only 3 of 15 timeframe × target settings were positive, and all three ~4-year thirds lost. The long side's small gain is the 2010–21 bull market; shorts lost.
lesson: A vendor result built on unpublished rules and a 6-month holdout can't be checked; screen pre-declared readings over a long history and compare with the same trade at the same minute on random days.
summary: "Liquidity sweep, then the gap flips": entering after price takes out the previous hour's high or low and a fair-value gap forms (or an old one is broken) did no better than the same trade at the same time on random days, over 11 years of Nasdaq futures.

title: Twenty classic Bitcoin strategies vs buy & hold, with the last third of the data locked away
source: A research brief written for an online strategy-builder
timeframe: one signal timeframe per strategy (1h/4h/1d/1w); fixed exits only; fills walked on 30m bars
headline: 0 of 672 configurations across 20 concepts passed the brief's rules (≥100 trades, drawdown < 20%, profit factor > 1.1, beat buy & hold) on 2017–2023, so nothing reached the hidden third. Buy & hold made +609% with an 84% drawdown; the best config under 20% drawdown made +291%.
why: Beating +609% at 1x without ever losing 20% needs ~39%/yr for six years at a Calmar near 2. Many concepts had a real edge (profit factor 1.4–2.5) but every one that out-earned buy & hold drew down ≥34.6%, and adding shorts made every family worse after costs.
lesson: On an asset that rose 7x, "beat buy & hold with drawdown < 20%" is a Calmar requirement, not an edge test; check the return-vs-drawdown frontier before building more variants.
summary: Twenty well-known Bitcoin strategies, with fees and slippage included, were asked to make more than buy & hold while never losing 20%. None did. The best low-drawdown rule made +291% while buy & hold made +609%, and everything that beat buy & hold lost at least a third of the account along the way.

title: Nasdaq 30-minute breakout of the highest close of 34 bars, with an ADX filter, out at the close
source: A breakout-strategy X account, which posted its TradeStation code
timeframe: 30m bars (24h session), buy stop at the highest close of 34 bars, entries 08:00–15:00 Chicago, $1,000 stop, exit at the session close
headline: No performance numbers were published, only "keeps performing year after year". The rule as coded makes +2.9bp per trade on 11 years of NQ (1,561 trades, Sharpe 0.48, interval includes 0, vs buy & hold 1.03), but simply being long at the same minute on random days with the same filter state makes +3.3bp (40th percentile).
why: The profit is the 2010–21 intraday upward drift, not the breakout: every short version loses, the first half of the sample is negative, and ES (+2.9bp) also sits inside its own random-day control (79th percentile). The dollar results grow every year because Nasdaq went from 1,800 to 14,700 while the stop stayed at a fixed $1,000.
lesson: Read "$ per contract, every year" results in basis points: a rising price level and a fixed-dollar stop make any long rule look better each year. For long-only index rules, compare with a long at the same minute on random days that pass the same filters.
summary: A breakout of the highest 30-minute close of the last 17 hours, posted as one that "keeps performing year after year", made money on 11 years of Nasdaq futures — but no more than buying at the same time of day on random days. Its growing yearly dollar profits came from Nasdaq's rising price, not from the breakout.

title: Nasdaq pre-market range reversal: after one side breaks, trade back to the other end for 50 points
source: A day-trading account on X, pitching it as better than the opening-range breakout
timeframe: 1m, range 08:12–09:12 New York, entries by 15:00, flat at the 16:00 close
data: NQ / ES 1m Globex 2010-06→2021-09 (2,910 days); NQ 5m 2025-05→2026-04 at the post's price level
headline: No numbers were published. Our replication on 12 years of NQ lost money before costs in every reading: the main version (fade the break once price closes back inside) made −0.22bp per trade gross, −1.36bp net over 2,667 trades, with 0 of 12 years positive.
why: Random entries at the same minute on other days do as well or better, and trading WITH the break on the same stop and target is about as bad, so the break tells you nothing about direction. The "double break every day" is half true: one side breaks almost every day (the pre-market hour is narrow), both sides on 63% of days.
lesson: A fixed point target ("50 pts on NQ") is a 2.8% move at 2010 prices and 0.17% today; scale it to price before testing on a long history, then test the literal number on the post's own recent price level.
summary: An X post said marking the 8:12–9:12 pre-market range on Nasdaq futures and fading the first break for 50 points beats the opening-range breakout "every single day". Over 12 years of Nasdaq and S&P futures, every version lost money, mostly before costs, and random entries did as well.
